title: Eldorado Springs Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Eldorado Springs wells have a 49-ft median depth, but local records range to 1,989 feet. See yield, water levels, risks and costs.
intro_html: Buying land or a home in Eldorado Springs means looking beyond whether a property has a well permit. The records within five miles include 3,866 Colorado DWR permits, but only 1,487 are recorded as constructed, 1,685 report total depth, 324 report pump yield, and 73 report static water level. That uneven reporting matters. The available data shows a shallow median depth of 49 feet, a median reported yield of 10.0 gallons per minute, and a median static water level of 12 feet below the surface. Those figures are useful for planning, but they do not guarantee what a new well will find on a particular lot.

sections.heading: Eldorado Springs Well Depth Depends on the Ground
sections.html:
The reported median well depth near Eldorado Springs is 49 feet. The middle half runs from 20 to 300 feet, so nearby wells vary sharply even before considering the deepest record of 1,989 feet. Depth distribution tells the same story: 56% are under 100 feet, 17% are 100 to 300 feet, 22% are 300 to 600 feet, and 5% exceed 600 feet.

For a drilling bid, do not use the 49-foot median as a promise. It is a starting point for a shallow local pattern, while the 20-to-300-foot middle range shows how much uncertainty remains. Permits identify many wells in unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, along with Alluvial and Laramie Fox Hills entries. Fractured rock can change quickly from lot to lot.

sections.heading: What Eldorado Springs Wells Usually Produce
sections.html:
Reported well yield is strongest in the 5-to-15-gallon-per-minute range. The median is 10.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 6.5 to 13.3. A further 21% report more than 15 gallons per minute, while 15% fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute and 1% are under 1 gallon per minute.

That low-yield tail is small, but it is important to a buyer because a property may still need storage and careful demand planning. A yield test is not the same as a guarantee of household performance during every season. Review the well construction report, pump test, permitted use, and any storage or treatment equipment. An exempt household-use well is generally subject to Colorado’s 35-gallon-per-minute pumping limit.

sections.heading: Water Levels Near Eldorado Springs and Their Trend
sections.html:
The reported median static water level is 12 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 6 to 40 feet. That is a relatively shallow measured water level in the available records, but the sample is limited to 73 wells reporting static water level. A nearby measurement is useful context, not a substitute for testing the well you may buy.

The decade series shows a median of 8 feet below the surface in the 2010s and 10 feet in the 2020s. That is a deeper reported median in the newer decade, but the facts do not establish a long-term dropping water table. Measurement dates, locations, well construction, and the small reporting pool can all affect the comparison. Ask for current water-level information during due diligence.

sections.heading: Permit History and Drillers Around Eldorado Springs
sections.html:
Colorado DWR records show permits issued into the 2020s, with the newest permit year listed as 2025. There are 37 permits from the 2020s in the supplied decade summary. The record is not a complete list of active production wells: monitoring use accounts for 47% of the use mix, domestic or household use for 35%, stock for 2%, and irrigation for 1%.

The most active drillers named in these records are Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 1,002 entries; Boyles Bros. Drilling Co. (Lensch, George E), with 410; and Ground Water Systems Inc (Wilson, Richard R.), with 182. Those counts describe permit records, not endorsements or current availability. Confirm licensing, insurance, scope, and references before hiring anyone.

sections.heading: Eldorado Springs Well Drilling Cost
sections.html:
The local drilling model uses a typical rate of $50 to $70 per foot in Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the 49-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $2,400 to $3,400. That is only the hole. A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $8,400 to $15,400.

Your bid can move outside that range if the site requires substantially more depth, difficult access, extra casing or grout, rock excavation, or specialized equipment. The depth distribution is the reason to ask how a contractor handles a dry hole or an unsuccessful interval before work starts. Get the drilling, completion, pump, electrical, trenching, testing, and permit responsibilities written into the proposal.

sections.heading: Risks to Check Before Building Near Eldorado Springs
sections.html:
Yield and depth are not the only concerns. Within about ten miles, the mapped environment includes 193 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 326 historic mine features, and 23 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These maps do not prove that a particular parcel is contaminated, but they justify a records search and water testing appropriate to the property’s location and history.

Ask about dry holes, low-yield wells, casing, grout, and the condition of the pump system. Confirm that the well permit allows the intended use and that the septic layout can meet setbacks from the well, property lines, surface water, and the proposed building. In mountain terrain, access for a rig, trenching route, slope stability, and winter construction can affect both feasibility and cost.

sections.heading: Due Diligence for an Eldorado Springs Lot
sections.html:
Start with the well permit and construction report, then compare the property with nearby records in Paragon Estates, Superior, Boulder, Louisville, Valmont, and Coal Creek. A cluster of nearby wells can help frame expected depth and yield, but it cannot replace a site-specific evaluation, particularly where fractured-bedrock conditions are involved.

For an existing home, inspect the pump, pressure tank, wiring, storage, treatment equipment, and recent water-quality results. For vacant land, have a driller and septic professional review access, the proposed building envelope, and the likely well and septic locations before closing. Keep contingencies for well yield, water quality, permits, and septic approval. The numbers here are planning evidence, not a promise of water on any individual parcel.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Eldorado Springs?
faq.a: The median reported depth within five miles of Eldorado Springs is 49 feet. The middle half runs from 20 to 300 feet, and the deepest record is 1,989 feet. Most are under 100 feet, but 22% are 300 to 600 feet and 5% exceed 600 feet. A local driller should price the lot-specific uncertainty.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Eldorado Springs?
faq.a: The drilling model uses $50 to $70 per foot. At the 49-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $2,400 to $3,400. A finished well including pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $8,400 to $15,400. Difficult access, greater depth, casing, grout, and dry-hole risk can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Eldorado Springs wells produce?
faq.a: The median reported yield is 10.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 6.5 to 13.3. Most reported wells, 63%, produce 5 to 15 gallons per minute. However, 15% report 1 to 5 gallons per minute and 1% are under 1 gallon per minute, so review the actual well test before relying on the supply.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Eldorado Springs?
faq.a: The records alone cannot establish that a property’s water is safe. Within about ten miles are 193 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 326 historic mine features, and 23 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those facts support property-specific testing and a review of nearby land uses, mine history, well construction, and treatment needs before purchase.

faq.q: Are water levels dropping near Eldorado Springs?
faq.a: The reported median static water level was 8 feet below the surface in the 2010s and 10 feet in the 2020s. That newer value is deeper, but the available facts do not prove a declining water table because only 73 wells report static water level and the measurements may differ by location, construction, and timing. Request current measurements for the property.
